name: Jade Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for seeing me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, so no links to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. Everything here is confidential, and I'm interested in both what you'd say publicly and what you actually think. Could you describe a normal working day for me?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach English at St Aldric's, a secondary school on the edge of town, about 900 kids. This is my second full year. I've got two Year 7 classes, two Year 9, and a Year 10 GCSE group, which is the one that scares me because their results count. Most of my day is reading aloud, getting them to write, and then marking what they've written, which is the part that never ends.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How much marking are we talking about?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: On a bad week, maybe a hundred and twenty essays. I mark by hand, with a green pen, because that's how I was taught and I think kids read handwritten comments more. My boyfriend Sam, who's an electrician, jokes that I spend more evenings with Year 9 than with him. He's not wrong. I've never used any of the AI stuff; I don't trust it with a kid's writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, I never needed it anyway. In the English department we'd have a laugh about all the training days we sat through for nothing. I'm not online much, so I wouldn't post anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, even if AI is hype, I'm worried. The school brought in an AI marking pilot this year for Year 7 spelling and grammar, and the head likes it. If it saves time, they'll expect us to use it, and I'll look like the slow one who refuses. And I'm still not a strong teacher yet, my Year 10 results last summer were below the department average.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep marking by hand, but I'd try to get faster with a proper rubric instead of writing essays back to kids. I'd keep the £3,000 we've got saved and not touch it. Maybe I'd look at the AI marking pilot once, just so I can say I tried it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not because of the robots, because I'm not sure I'm good enough at this job yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd look at the pilot 'just so you can say you tried'. Why does that matter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because Mr Hayes, my head of department, asked twice and I said no twice. In my second year as a teacher, I can't afford to look stubborn about the school's AI marking pilot. I'd do one session, smile, and go back to my green pen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's money like at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine-ish. Sam earns more than me and we split rent fifty-fifty on a small terraced house, which is a stretch for me. If the boiler goes again this winter, that's half our savings gone.

say: I'd say I **never needed** AI for my marking anyway.
I'd laugh with the department about wasted **training days**.
think: The school's **AI marking pilot** could make me look like the slow one.
My **Year 10 results** were below average, and that worries me more.
do: Keep **marking by hand** but get faster with a proper rubric.
Try the **marking pilot** once so my boss sees I tried.
feel: **Uneasy** about whether she's **good enough** at the job yet.
S0.quote: In my second year as a teacher, I can't afford to look stubborn about the school's AI marking pilot.
fieldNote: Her worry in this world is her **own skill**, not AI.
She'd go through the **motions** of the pilot to protect herself.
Her **green pen** is both a teaching belief and a comfort habit.

steps.text: Keep marking essays by hand with a shorter rubric
Attend one session of the AI marking pilot
Leave the £3,000 joint savings untouched for the boiler

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI can't read a fourteen-year-old's poem and understand what they meant. I'd probably say it in a staff meeting, quietly. And I'd say teaching isn't a writing task, it's a people task.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it scares me. Writing and checking are what English teachers do most of the day, and I'm the newest one in our department. If software marks the essays and plans the lessons, then the head can give one English teacher more classes, and the newest ones go first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start applying for jobs at other schools now, before anything is cut, especially the girls' grammar school across town, which is big on handwritten exams. I'd stop eating out and put another £100 a month away. I'd probably have to learn the marking tool too, even though I hate it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Like someone's slowly taking the floor away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if your post was cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really anyone. The head has a budget, the government sets the budget, and if a tool is cheaper, they'll use it. I'd blame myself a bit too, for not being better faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the tool even though you hate it. What would that look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sitting with Priya, who's in her fourth year and uses all of it, for an hour after school. She'd show me, I'd take notes, and I'd try it on one Year 7 class only. If the kids' writing gets worse, I'd go back to the pen.

say: I'd say AI **can't understand** a teenager's poem.
I'd say teaching is a **people task**, not a writing task.
think: **Writing and checking** are most of an English teacher's day.
I'm the **newest** in my department, so I'd go first.
do: Apply now to the **grammar school** across town.
Stop eating out and save **£100 more** a month.
Learn the **marking tool** with a colleague, on one Year 7 class.
feel: **Anxious**, like the **floor** is slowly being taken away.
S1.quote: Writing and checking are what English teachers do most of the day, and I'm the newest one in our department.
fieldNote: She sees her subject as **right in the line** of thinking AI.
She blames no one outside, partly **herself**, which fits her centre outlook.
Her escape plan is a school that values **handwritten exams**.

steps.text: Apply for an English post at the girls' grammar school
Stop eating out and add £100 a month to savings
Try the marking tool with Priya on one Year 7 class

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government needs to stop this, or at least slow it down for schools. I'd sign whatever petition came round. At work I'd try to sound brave for the kids, but I'm not a good actor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd lose my job, or most of it. If AI can do any thinking work by 2028, it can teach Shakespeare better than a second-year teacher with below-average results. Schools would keep a few experienced teachers to manage the rooms, and I'm not experienced. I'd be twenty-nine with an English degree in a world that doesn't need English teachers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I honestly don't know where I'd start, and that's the scary part. I'd probably apply for a teaching assistant job if one came up, or ask about cover supervisor work, because that's just being in the room. I'd cut everything, the car, the phone contract, and ask Sam if we could move somewhere cheaper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Sick, really. I'd lie awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Sam's work is hands-on. Does the 2031 robot date matter to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's the only thing that makes it bearable. If Sam has three more years of work as an electrician, then at least one of us is earning while I figure it out. But I'd feel awful leaning on him, because we're not even married.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your Year 10s?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them their writing still matters, even if a machine can do it. I'd mean it, but I wouldn't know how to prove it. The kid in my Year 10 group who wants to be a journalist, I wouldn't know what to tell her.

say: I'd say the government should **slow it down** for schools, at least for now.
I'd sign any **petition** that came round.
think: I expect to **lose my job**, or most of it, by 2028.
Schools would keep a few **experienced teachers**, and I'm not one.
do: Apply for **teaching assistant** or cover supervisor work.
Cut the **car and phone contract** straight away.
Ask my partner about **moving somewhere cheaper**.
S2.quote: I'd be twenty-nine with an English degree in a world that doesn't need English teachers.
fieldNote: She has **no plan**, and says so plainly.
Her partner's **hands-on trade** and the 2031 robot date are her lifeline.
She feels uneasy **leaning on** a partner she isn't married to.

steps.text: Apply for cover supervisor or teaching assistant posts
Sell the car and drop to a cheaper phone plan
Lean on Sam's electrician pay for the household bills
Move with Sam to a cheaper rented house

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as the fast one, that schools need protecting, but I'd say it with less panic. Maybe I'd go to a union meeting for once. Not to make speeches, just to listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is better, but I'm resistant to change, I know that about myself. I'd probably spend the first two years hoping it wasn't true. By 2031 I'd be in my seventh year and maybe better at the job, but still an English teacher in a world where AI writes better than everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd try to move towards the part that's about people. Maybe pastoral work, being a form tutor who actually knows the kids, or doing a course in mentoring. I'd save hard for two years, and Sam and I would put off any wedding talk until we knew what was happening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a bit of air. I could breathe in that one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd spend two years hoping it wasn't true. Is that what you'd actually do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes. I'm being honest. I'm a creature of habit, and I'd need someone to sit me down and say it's happening, start now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would that someone be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My mum, probably. She was made redundant from a bank call centre when I was at school, and she always says she waited too long. She'd tell me not to make the same mistake.

say: I'd ask for schools to be **protected**, with less panic.
I might go to a **union meeting** just to listen.
think: I'd probably spend **two years hoping** it wasn't true.
Even by 2031 I'd be an English teacher where **AI writes better**.
do: Move towards **pastoral work** and a mentoring course.
Save hard for **two years** before anything lands.
Put **wedding talk** on hold until it's clearer.
S3.quote: I'm a creature of habit, and I'd need someone to sit me down and say it's happening, start now.
fieldNote: She openly predicts her own **delay** in reacting.
Her mum's **redundancy story** is the warning she'd listen to.
Wedding plans are the first thing she'd **pause**.

steps.text: Take a short course in pastoral mentoring for teenagers
Save £150 a month for two years
Hold off on wedding plans with Sam until 2030
Wait a year or two to see whether it's real

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for schools to work it out, and that teachers will still be needed. I'd probably believe that in public, more or less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years means I'd have time to get properly good, maybe even head of English somewhere small. But I'd still be in a subject that's mostly writing, and that's the thing AI does best. I think I'd be fine for most of the decade and then not fine at the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep teaching and get better, honestly that's my plan for the next few years anyway. I'd look at a second subject, maybe drama, because it's more about bodies and voices in a room. And Sam and I would probably get married in 2028 like we'd talked about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious, a quieter version. A worry in the back of my head.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why drama?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because you can't do drama on a screen, not properly. I did it at school and loved it, and the department at St Aldric's is just one woman who's retiring soon. It feels like a door that would still be open in 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything that would stop you doing it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Me, mostly. I'd keep putting it off. If the school offered to pay for the course, I'd do it; if I had to pay, I'd probably wait.

say: I'd say **ten years** is plenty for schools to adapt.
I'd say English teachers will **still be needed** in classrooms.
think: I'd be **fine for most** of the decade, then not fine at the end.
My subject is **mostly writing**, which AI does best.
do: Keep teaching and **get better** at the job.
Train in **drama** as a second subject.
feel: **Anxious** in a quieter way, a worry at the back of her **mind**.
S4.quote: You can't do drama on a screen, not properly.
fieldNote: Ten years delays her fear but doesn't **remove** it.
Drama is her picture of a **door that stays open**.
She'd only retrain if the **school paid** for it.

steps.text: Keep teaching English and aim for better Year 10 results
Take a drama teaching course if St Aldric's pays

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. I'd have no time and no plan, and I'm not someone who changes fast. What would help is someone, the school or the government, paying for teachers to retrain into the people side of the job, and telling us early and straight, not with a glossy training day.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Whether I'd still choose teaching. And the answer is yes, I think. I wish I'd known all this before I spent three years on an English degree.

headlineQuote: I wish I'd known all this before I spent three years on an English degree.
portrait: Jade is a second-year **English teacher** at a secondary school who marks by hand.
She lives with her **electrician boyfriend**, splitting rent on a small house, with £3,000 saved.
She doubts her **own skill** even before AI, and avoids new tools.
Her mood climbs to **alarmed** in the 2028 world, where she has no plan.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she'd have **no time** and no **plan**.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **retraining** into the people side of teaching.
Being told **early and straight**, not through a glossy training day.
